hints: Think about what you would see if chlorine, bromine and iodine each mixed with hydrogen, which reaction is explosive and which needs heating or barely reacts.
Link that trend to how strongly each halogen atom attracts an electron to form a 1- ion, considering shielding and nuclear charge down Group 17.
walkthrough:
Picture the reactions getting calmer**
Imagine hydrogen mixed with each halogen. Chlorine reacts explosively in sunlight, bromine needs heat and reacts more slowly, iodine is even slower and reversible. So vigour clearly falls down the group.

See the reaction as electron gain**
Forming $\text{HX}$ from $\text{X}_2$ involves each halogen atom gaining one electron to become $\text{X}^-$. A good oxidising agent gains electrons easily. Chlorine does this very readily, iodine much less so.

Explain why electron gain gets harder**
Down the group the atom gets larger with more shielding. Although nuclear charge increases, the extra shielding outweighs it, so the effective attraction for an incoming electron falls. Electronegativity decreases, oxidising power decreases, reactivity with hydrogen decreases.

Final answer: Reactivity with hydrogen becomes less vigorous down the group from chlorine to iodine.
Electronegativity decreases / halogens become weaker oxidising agents down the group, so they gain electrons less readily.

hints: Recall that $\text{SiCl}_4$ is readily hydrolysed by water to give a white solid oxide and steamy acidic fumes.
walkthrough:
Identify the hydrolysis products**
$\text{SiCl}_4$ reacts vigorously with water. Silicon forms its oxide, $\text{SiO}_2$, and all four chlorides are replaced by oxygen and released as $\text{HCl}$ gas which forms misty fumes in moist air.

Balance the atoms**
You need $2\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to supply $2\text{O}$ for $\text{SiO}_2$ and $4\text{H}$ for $4\text{HCl}$: $$\text{SiCl}_4 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{SiO}_2 + 4\text{HCl}$$

hints: Check oxidation numbers in the products, in which case does sulfur change from +6 in $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ to +4 in $\text{SO}_2$ and bromine change from -1 to 0 in $\text{Br}_2$.
Recall that $\text{NaCl}$ with concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ gives only $\text{HCl}$ and $\text{NaHSO}_4$ with no change in oxidation number.
Think about why bromide can be oxidised further but chloride cannot, linking to reducing strength increasing down Group 17.
walkthrough:
Classify the chloride reaction**
$$\text{NaCl} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{NaHSO}_4 + \text{HCl}$$ Oxidation numbers stay the same: $\text{Cl}$ is -1 on both sides, $\text{S}$ stays +6. This is simply proton transfer, so acid-base only.

Classify the bromide reaction**
With $\text{NaBr}$ you first get $\text{HBr}$ by acid-base reaction, but then $\text{HBr}$ is oxidised: $$2\text{HBr} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{Br}_2 + \text{SO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ Here $\text{Br}$ goes from -1 to 0 and $\text{S}$ goes from +6 to +4. So both acid-base and redox occur.

Explain the difference**
Bromide is a stronger reducing agent than chloride. Concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is a strong oxidising agent, strong enough to oxidise $\text{HBr}$ / $\text{Br}^-$ to $\text{Br}_2$, but not strong enough to oxidise $\text{HCl}$ / $\text{Cl}^-$ to $\text{Cl}_2$ under these conditions.

Final answer: NaCl + concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$: acid-base only.
NaBr + concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$: acid-base and redox.
Concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is strong enough to oxidise $\text{Br}^-$ / $\text{HBr}$ to $\text{Br}_2$ (itself reduced to $\text{SO}_2$) but cannot oxidise $\text{Cl}^-$ / $\text{HCl}$.

hints: Focus on which bond must break for decomposition, $\text{H-Cl}$ or $\text{H-I}$, and how bond length and strength change down the group.
walkthrough:
Compare the bonds that must break**
Decomposition $2\text{HX} \rightarrow \text{H}_2 + \text{X}_2$ requires breaking the $\text{H-X}$ bond. Chlorine is small so $\text{H-Cl}$ is short and strong. Iodine is large so $\text{H-I}$ is long and weak.

Link to heat energy**
A Bunsen flame provides enough energy to break the weaker $\text{H-I}$ bond but not enough to break the much stronger $\text{H-Cl}$ bond. Hence $\text{HI}$ decomposes and $\text{HCl}$ does not.
Final answer: The $\text{H-Cl}$ bond is stronger than the $\text{H-I}$ bond / bond enthalpy decreases down the group, so $\text{HCl}$ does not decompose on heating whereas $\text{HI}$ does.

hints: Recall the Bronsted-Lowry definition in terms of what particle is donated, not in terms of $\text{H}_2$ or electrons.
Think about what the word strong adds, what fraction of molecules split into ions in water.
walkthrough:
Define the Bronsted-Lowry acid part**
A Bronsted-Lowry acid is a proton donor. When $\text{HBr}$ dissolves, it donates $\text{H}^+$ to water: $$\text{HBr} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{H}_3\text{O}^+ + \text{Br}^-$$

Add the meaning of strong**
Strong means essentially complete dissociation in water. Every $\text{HBr}$ molecule transfers its proton, so $\text{[H}^+\text{]}$ equals the initial acid concentration.

Final answer: A proton / $\text{H}^+$ donor.
That fully dissociates / ionises in aqueous solution.

hints: Calculate the starting pH of $0.1 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{HBr}$, a strong acid, and note both flasks contain the same acid at the start.
Work out the equivalence volume when moles of base added equal moles of acid present ($25 \text{ cm}^3$ of $0.1 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$).
Think about the final excess reagent, strong alkali $\text{NaOH}$ gives very high pH but weak base $\text{NH}_3$ gives only mildly alkaline pH.
walkthrough:
Fix the start and the vertical**
$0.1 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{HBr}$ is fully dissociated so $\text{[H}^+\text{]} = 0.1$, pH = 1. Both titrations start at pH 1 or just below. Moles acid = $0.025 \times 0.1$. With $0.1 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ base, equivalence needs $25 \text{ cm}^3$. Draw a classic S shape with a steep rise through $25 \text{ cm}^3$.

Draw the strong base finish**
For $\text{NaOH}$ plus $\text{HBr}$, strong acid with strong base, excess $\text{NaOH}$ drives pH to about 13. Your curve climbs steeply through pH 7 at $25 \text{ cm}^3$ then levels above pH 12.

Draw the weak base finish**
For $\text{NH}_3$ plus $\text{HBr}$, strong acid with weak base, equivalence is acidic (pH below 7) and excess weak base only reaches about pH 9 to 11. So the top plateau is clearly lower, in the 8 to 12 range, with a shorter vertical.

Final answer: Both curves: sigmoid with sharp vertical at $25 \text{ cm}^3$, starting at pH about 1.
NaOH curve finishes at pH >12 in excess alkali.
NH3 curve finishes at pH 8 to 12 in excess ammonia.

hints: Identify the electrophile in $\text{H-Br}$, which end is $\delta^+$ and will be attacked by the $\text{C=C}$ pi electrons.
Remember the first curly arrow always starts at the double bond and points to the $\text{H}$, while a second arrow breaks $\text{H-Br}$ onto $\text{Br}$.
Decide which carbon gets the $\text{H}$ to leave the more stable secondary carbocation, then show $\text{Br}^-$ donating to that positive carbon.
Check you have shown dipoles, lone pair on $\text{Br}^-$, charges on the carbocation, and drawn the major product 2-bromopropane.
walkthrough:
Set up the electrophilic attack**
$\text{HBr}$ is polarised $\delta^+\text{H-Br}\delta^-$ because Br is more electronegative. The pi electrons of propene, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CH}_2$, act as a nucleophile. Draw a curly arrow from the $\text{C=C}$ to the $\text{H}$ of $\text{HBr}$, and a second curly arrow from the $\text{H-Br}$ bond onto $\text{Br}$ to make $\text{Br}^-$.

Form the most stable carbocation**
$\text{H}$ adds to the terminal $\text{CH}_2$ so the positive charge lands on the middle carbon, giving the secondary carbocation $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}^+\text{CH}_3$. Show the + charge on carbon. This is the intermediate.

Capture by bromide**
Draw the lone pair on $:\text{Br}^-$ with a curly arrow from that lone pair to the carbocation carbon. This forms the $\text{C-Br}$ bond.

Draw the major product**
The product is 2-bromopropane, $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{CHBr}$ or $\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_3$. Check all arrows, $\delta^+$ and $\delta^-$, lone pairs and charges are included.

Final answer: Step 1: $\text{C=C}$ attacks $\delta^+\text{H-Br}\delta^-$, $\text{H-Br}$ bond breaks to $\text{Br}^-$ forming $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{CH}^+$ carbocation.
Step 2: $:\text{Br}^-$ attacks carbocation to give $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{CHBr}$ (2-bromopropane). Full curly arrows, dipoles, lone pairs and charges shown.

hints: Compare the two possible intermediates, a secondary carbocation $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{CH}^+$ versus a primary carbocation $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2^+$.
Think about how alkyl groups push electron density toward the positive carbon to spread the charge.
walkthrough:
Name the competing intermediates**
Adding $\text{H}^+$ to the middle carbon gives a primary carbocation $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2^+$. Adding $\text{H}^+$ to the end carbon gives a secondary carbocation $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{CH}^+$. Only one pathway dominates.

Use the inductive effect to choose**
Alkyl groups donate electron density by the positive inductive effect (+I). The secondary cation has two methyl groups feeding electrons to the $\text{C}^+$, spreading the charge more effectively than the single ethyl group in the primary cation. Lower energy intermediate forms faster, so 2-bromopropane is the major product.

Final answer: The $2^\circ$ carbocation is more stable than the $1^\circ$ carbocation.
Due to greater positive inductive effect from two methyl groups compared to one ethyl group, stabilising the positive charge.

hints: Recall that aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ favours replacement of $\text{Br}$ by $\text{OH}$ to make an alcohol.
Recall that ethanolic $\text{NaOH}$ favours removal of $\text{HBr}$ to make an alkene, with water also formed.
walkthrough:
Assign the aqueous products**
In water, $\text{OH}^-$ acts as a nucleophile and substitutes $\text{Br}$: $$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH} + \text{NaBr}$$ So propan-1-ol plus sodium bromide.

Assign the ethanolic products**
In ethanol, $\text{OH}^-$ acts as a base and eliminates $\text{HBr}$: $$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH=CH}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{NaBr}$$ So propene plus water plus sodium bromide.

Final answer: In water: organic $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ / propan-1-ol, inorganic $\text{NaBr}$.
In ethanol: organic $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CH}_2$ / propene, inorganic $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and $\text{NaBr}$.
